title: Amounts are reported in euros unless changed
rule: Scope converts every amount into one reporting currency. That currency is EUR unless the Scope Settings sheet or a setting changed in Scope says otherwise. The Holdings FX rates are always rates against EUR, so Scope warns when the base currency is set to anything else (amounts would mix currencies) and points you to the display currency instead.
example: A GBP loan of 10m at a rate of 0.855 GBP per EUR is reported as EUR 11.70m.
code: baseCurrency: 'EUR',
tests: total exposure equals an independent recomputation from the raw Holdings grid (Σ nominal ÷ FX rate)
FX: direction verified against the RC column; display currency scales; the exceptions apply only where configured

title: Scope works out which way FX rates are quoted
rule: Unless you change the FX quote setting, Scope tries both dividing and multiplying each amount by its rate, and keeps whichever reproduces the extract's reference-currency (RC) column. The workbook itself always divides.
example: For a GBP 10m position with rate 0.855 and an RC column showing EUR 11.70m, dividing matches, so Scope reads the rate as GBP per EUR and divides.
code: // 'auto': test both against the RC (reference-currency) column and use the one that reproduces it.
tests: FX: direction verified against the RC column; display currency scales; the exceptions apply only where configured
confirm: Should Scope keep working out the direction from the RC column? If not, it will always divide by the rate as the workbook does, which would be wrong for an extract that quotes EUR per currency.

title: One FX rate per currency, as in the workbook
rule: Unless you change the FX rate source setting, Scope converts every position in a currency at one rate: the rate on the FX reference investor's first Holdings row in that currency (the workbook's Calculations columns CU:CW). The other choice, each position's own rate, uses the rate on each row.
example: If Investor 1's first GBP row shows 0.855 and another GBP row shows 0.90, both rows are converted at 0.855.
code: fxRateSource: 'workbook',
tests: FX: direction verified against the RC column; display currency scales; the exceptions apply only where configured
FX: the workbook rule uses one rate per currency (the reference investor's first row); a currency it does not hold falls back with a warning

title: Drawn is blank in "incl. part in funds" views
rule: For a view named after an investor followed by "incl. part in funds", Scope leaves the drawn amount blank, as the workbook does (its drawn block has no such column and shows #N/A). If you set Look-through drawn to show, Scope calculates it.
example: In the view "Investor 1 incl. part in funds", exposure is shown and drawn is blank.
code: lookThroughDrawn: 'blank',
tests: incl. part in funds, as filled in practice: shares in the column row plus "100%" of itself in the incl. row; a region's incl. row without the region; drawn blank as the workbook

title: Scope works out the nominal column's currency
rule: Unless you change it, Scope decides for each workbook whether the nominal column is in the position's own (quotation) currency or already in EUR, by checking nominal against drawn plus unfunded. Unless you change those settings, Scope takes drawn and commitment as quotation currency and divides them by the rate, as the workbook does.
example: On a GBP row with nominal 11.70m, rate 0.855 and drawn plus unfunded of GBP 10m, nominal × 0.855 gives 10m, so Scope treats the nominal as already in EUR and does not convert it again.
code: nominalIn: 'auto', drawnIn: 'qc', commitmentIn: 'qc',
tests: amount currency: a nominal column already in EUR on non-EUR rows is detected (nominal × rate = drawn + unfunded), read as EUR and not converted twice; the setting overrides
confirm: Should Scope keep working out the nominal column's currency for each workbook? The alternative is to always treat it as the position's own currency, like drawn and commitment, which would convert nominals that are already in EUR a second time.

title: Which investor sets FX rates if none is named
rule: If the FX reference investor setting is blank, Scope uses the first investor column listed in Mapping column H (the list of views). If there is none, it uses the first investor in Funding Name.
example: If Mapping H lists "Total platform", "Investor 1", "Investor 2", Scope takes FX rates from Investor 1.
code: fxReferenceInvestor: '',          // investor column (Mapping!Z name or display name); blank = the first investor column in Mapping H (§7), else the first of...
tests: FX: direction verified against the RC column; display currency scales; the exceptions apply only where configured
Ownership grid: only the "incl. part in funds" views the workbook lists exist; a platform-total row is ignored; FX reference = first column in Mapping H
confirm: Is the first investor column in Mapping H the right one to take FX rates from when none is named? Every currency's rate would come from that investor's first row in that currency.

title: IG cut-off is a rating score of 610
rule: Scope marks a position SUB IG when its rating score is above 610, on the Mapping AC:AD scale where a higher score is weaker. A score of 610 or below is IG.
example: A score of 610 is IG; a score of 611 is SUB IG.
code: igThreshold: 610,                 // rating score strictly above this = SUB IG (Mapping!AC:AD scale; higher = weaker)
tests: ratings: internal unless NR, worst agency otherwise, odd dashes normalised, IG threshold 610
view formulas: parsed as the workbook writes them, may name another view, keep their coefficients as typed, and fail loudly

title: "SINGLE" means the Portfolio is the investor code
rule: When Holdings › Model Portfolio says "SINGLE", Scope uses the Portfolio value as the investor code instead.
example: A row with Model Portfolio "SINGLE" and Portfolio "61007" gets investor code 61007.
code: singleToken: 'SINGLE',            // Holdings: Model Portfolio = SINGLE → use Portfolio as the investor code
tests: SINGLE: Model Portfolio = SINGLE uses Portfolio as the investor code

title: Amounts are shown in millions
rule: Scope divides amounts on the Output by 1,000,000, so they are shown in millions.
example: EUR 125,400,000 is shown as 125.4.
code: unit: 1e6,                        // Output amounts in millions
tests: total exposure equals an independent recomputation from the raw Holdings grid (Σ nominal ÷ FX rate)

title: Standard maturity buckets
rule: Unless you change them, Scope groups remaining life into 0-3, 3-5, 5-10, 10-20 and 20+ years.
example: A loan with 4.2 years left falls in "3-5 y".
confirm: Are 0-3, 3-5, 5-10, 10-20 and 20+ years the buckets you report? Any other split has to be set in the Scope Settings sheet or in Scope.

title: The attributed group is called "Group"
rule: Scope calls the attributed investor group "Group" in every label, such as "Group attributed" and the Group view, unless you rename it.
example: Labels read "Group attributed" and "Group share of book".
code: attributionLabel: 'Group',        // name of the attributed investor group in every label ("Group attributed", …)
tests: views: each view is a row of weights over the investor columns (the settings sheet); group + third party = total per asset
confirm: Should the label stay "Group", or be your firm's own name? It appears on every page and report that shows the attributed share.

title: Spreads below 20 are read as percent
rule: Unless you fix the spread unit, Scope reads a spread below 0.5 (but not 0) as a decimal rate and multiplies it by 10,000 to get bps. A spread from 0.5 to below 20 is read as a percentage and multiplied by 100. A spread of 20 or more is taken as bps already. Negative spreads follow the same steps by size.
example: 0.0185 becomes 185 bps, 1.85 becomes 185 bps and 185 stays 185 bps, but 19.5 becomes 1,950 bps.
code: spreadUnit: 'auto',               // 'bps' | 'percent' | 'auto' (values below 20 are read as percent and × 100)
confirm: Is "below 20 means percent" safe for your spreads? A 15 bps spread typed as 15 would show as 1,500 bps; if that can happen, the unit should be fixed to bps or percent.

title: Only Total platform exists as a ready-made view
rule: Without an Ownership sheet or Scope Settings sheet, the only combined view Scope knows is "Total platform", which adds up every investor column. A view with the same name as an investor column needs no definition.
example: With no Ownership sheet, "Total platform" and "Investor 1" both work, but "Region A" shows nothing.
code: views: { 'Total platform': '*' },
tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
confirm: Should "Total platform" (all investor columns) always exist as a view, even when Mapping H does not list it?

title: No investor types or ownership unless given
rule: Without an Ownership sheet, a Scope Settings sheet or a change made in Scope, Scope gives every investor column no type (shown as Unclassified) and no group ownership.
example: In a workbook without the Ownership tab, Investor 1 shows as Unclassified with ownership not set.
code: // entity, 0 = third party, 0.35 = a fund 35% held by the group). Types: Group entity, Fund, Third party, Mandate.
tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
confirm: Without an Ownership sheet no investor counts towards the group, so the Group view is empty. Is that right, rather than assuming 100%?

title: The workbook's special FX rate is not built in
rule: Scope does not copy the workbook's hard-coded FX exception. No position gets a special rate unless you add an FX Exception row giving the investor, currency, view, and a rate or Hardcoded column.
example: Without an FX Exception table, Investor 5's GBP positions in Region A are converted at the standard 0.855.
code: // `rate` (a number) or `column` (the name of a Hardcoded column holding one rate per asset) when `view` is selected.
tests: FX: direction verified against the RC column; display currency scales; the exceptions apply only where configured
confirm: Should the workbook's special FX rate apply only when you list it in the settings sheet? If the row is missing, those positions are converted at the standard rate with no warning.

title: Countries not listed go to Rest of world
rule: Scope puts any country that is not in its region list into "Rest of world".
example: A position in "Greece" or "United States" shows under Rest of world.
code: // Country → region for the region breakdown (countries not listed fall into 'Rest of world').
confirm: Is Rest of world right for every country outside the list, including European countries that are not listed, such as Greece?

title: United Kingdom and Ireland form one region
rule: In the region breakdown, Scope puts "United Kingdom" and "Ireland" into "UK & Ireland". The country must be spelt as listed, but capitals, spaces and punctuation don't matter, and a note in brackets at the end of the country is ignored.
example: A position in "Ireland" shows under UK & Ireland; so does one in "United Kingdom (England)". One in "UK" does not, because "UK" is not listed.
code: 'United Kingdom': 'UK & Ireland', Ireland: 'UK & Ireland',
confirm: Is UK & Ireland the grouping you want in the region breakdown? Check also how your workbook spells the UK, since "UK" or "Great Britain" would fall into Rest of world.

title: Countries in Continental Europe
rule: Scope puts France, Germany, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Switzerland, Austria, Poland and Luxembourg into "Continental Europe".
example: A position in "Poland" shows under Continental Europe; one in "Greece" does not, because Greece is not listed.
code: France: 'Continental Europe', Germany: 'Continental Europe', Spain: 'Continental Europe', Italy: 'Continental Europe', Netherlands: 'Continental Europe',
confirm: Should other European countries, such as Greece, the Czech Republic or the Baltic states, be added to Continental Europe? Today they fall into Rest of world.

title: Concentration limits are only examples
rule: The Concentration page compares the book with example limits, not mandate limits: single name 10%, sponsor 20%, sector 35%, country 30%, sub-IG 25% and non-base currency 40%.
example: If the largest single name is 12% of exposure, it is shown as above the 10% limit.
code: thresholds: { limit_single_name_pct: 10, limit_sponsor_pct: 20, limit_sector_pct: 35, limit_country_pct: 30, limit_sub_ig_pct: 25, limit_non_base_ccy_pct: 40 },
tests: concentration: thresholds status, headroom, worst contributor (illustrative config values)
concentration: demo book reconciles with the engine
confirm: What are your real mandate limits? Until these example figures (10/20/35/30/25/40%) are replaced, breaches shown on the Concentration page do not reflect the mandate.

title: Five investor types
rule: Scope lets each investor column be one of five types: Group entity, Partly owned, Fund, Third party or Mandate.
example: A fund 45% owned by the group has ownership 45% and type Partly owned, unless other investor columns hold its units, in which case it is a Fund.
code: AUM.INVESTOR_TYPES = ['Group entity', 'Partly owned', 'Fund', 'Third party', 'Mandate'];
tests: weights: 1, 0.35, 35%, 7/20 and =7/20 are all read; types are inferred from the ownership when the Type column is blank
views: each view is a row of weights over the investor columns (the settings sheet); group + third party = total per asset
confirm: Are these five types the classification you use? No other type can be chosen.

title: A "3-5" bucket stops just under 5 years
rule: Scope puts a remaining life in a bucket written "a-b" when it is at least a years and below b years, and adds " y" to the label. Scope checks the buckets in the order listed and uses the first that fits.
example: A loan with exactly 3.0 years left falls in "3-5 y", not "0-3 y"; one with 4.99 years left is also "3-5 y".
code: if (m && years >= +m[1] && years < +m[2]) return b + ' y';
tests: settings: a duplicated Investors row is reported and the first kept; a formula coefficient above 1 is a multiple while an ownership above 1 is a percentage; maturity buckets typed as text work
confirm: Should a loan with exactly 3.0 years left fall in 3-5 rather than 0-3?

title: A bucket like "20+" has no upper end
rule: Scope puts every remaining life of n years or more into a bucket written "n+".
example: With buckets ending in "20+", a loan with 25 years left falls in "20+ y".
code: if (p && years >= +p[1]) return b + ' y';
tests: settings: a duplicated Investors row is reported and the first kept; a formula coefficient above 1 is a multiple while an ownership above 1 is a percentage; maturity buckets typed as text work
confirm: Should the last bucket mean n years or more? A loan with exactly 20.0 years left falls in 20+, not 10-20.

title: Matured or Unknown when no bucket fits
rule: If a remaining life fits no bucket, Scope labels it "Matured" when it is negative and "Unknown" otherwise. A position with no maturity date is "Unknown".
example: A loan 0.5 years past maturity shows as Matured; one with no maturity date shows as Unknown; one with 25 years left, when the only buckets are 0-3 and 3-5, shows as Unknown.
code: return years < 0 ? 'Matured' : 'Unknown';
tests: settings: a duplicated Investors row is reported and the first kept; a formula coefficient above 1 is a multiple while an ownership above 1 is a percentage; maturity buckets typed as text work
confirm: Should a position past its maturity date show as Matured and still count in the totals, rather than being left out?

title: Deal details shown on the asset page
rule: Scope lists these details on the asset page: sector, subsector, country, region, sponsor, repayment type, cash-flow type, instrument, origination, deal year, deal lead, classification, financial close, watchlist, covenant compliance, IC date, funding date, protection end date, upfront fee (bps), total transaction size, transaction group, chronological order and description.

confirm: Is this the right list of deal details for the asset page? Anything not on it will not be shown there.

title: ESG details shown on the asset page
rule: Scope carries these ESG details for each asset: the ESG, E, S and G scores, GHG scopes 1, 2 and 3 (tonnes), GHG intensity (tonnes per EUR m), and the taxonomy sector and subsector.
example: The asset page's ESG box shows ESG score 72 and GHG scope 1 of 1,200 t.

confirm: Is this the right list of ESG details to show? Anything else in ESG Hardcoded will not appear on the asset page.

title: Which position values can be corrected by hand
rule: Scope lets you correct only these position values by hand: nominal, drawn, commitment, currency, FX rate, internal grade, Fitch, Moody's, S&P, maturity date, purchase date, rate type and spread.
example: If you correct a 10m nominal to 11m, totals rise by 1m and Scope keeps 10m as the original value.
code: AUM.ADJUSTABLE_POSITION_FIELDS = ['nominal', 'drawn', 'commitment', 'currency', 'fx_rate', 'internal_grade', 'fitch', 'moodys', 'sp', 'maturity_date', 'purch...
tests: corrections: a manual nominal moves the totals by the delta and keeps the original for the badge
confirm: Is this the right list? Anything else, such as WAL, country or sector, cannot be corrected by hand in Scope.

title: Asset values Scope reads as numbers
rule: Scope reads these asset values as numbers, not text: upfront fee (bps), total transaction size, deal year, WAL, chronological order, the ESG, E, S and G scores, GHG scopes 1 to 3 and GHG intensity.
example: An upfront fee typed as "0.75%" is read as the number 0.75, not as text.
code: AUM.NUMERIC_ASSET_FIELDS = ['upfront_fee_bps', 'total_transaction_size', 'deal_year', 'wal_years', 'chronological_order', 'esg_score', 'e_score', 's_score', ...
confirm: Are these the asset values that should be read as numbers? Any other value is kept as typed and cannot be added up or averaged.

title: An empty Scope Settings tab is ignored
rule: Scope uses the Scope Settings sheet only if it exists and has at least one row. An empty tab is ignored with no message.
example: With a blank "Scope Settings" tab, Scope uses its built-in settings.

tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
confirm: Is it fine that an empty Scope Settings tab is ignored without a message? A tab cleared by mistake would go unnoticed.

title: Changes made in Scope beat the workbook
rule: A setting changed in Scope wins over the Scope Settings sheet, which wins over Scope's built-in settings.
example: If the sheet says IG threshold 610 and you changed it to 400 in Scope, Scope uses 400.
code: const S = Object.assign({}, CONFIG, SS ? SS.scalars : {}, ov.settings || {}); // app changes to a setting win over the sheet
tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
view formulas: parsed as the workbook writes them, may name another view, keep their coefficients as typed, and fail loudly
confirm: Should a change made in the browser override the workbook's settings sheet? It means the workbook can say one thing while Scope uses another.

title: The Ownership sheet beats the Scope Settings sheet
rule: When a workbook has both an Ownership sheet and the older Scope Settings sheet, Scope takes ownership and views from the Ownership sheet. Scope Settings still supplies the FX exception and the settings.
example: If Scope Settings sets every ownership to 0 and the Ownership sheet says Investor 1 owns 100%, Scope uses 100%.

confirm: Is it right that the Ownership tab overrides the Scope Settings sheet for ownership and views? Any ownership or views left in Scope Settings would be ignored.

title: A grid edited in Scope replaces the Ownership sheet
rule: If you have edited the ownership grid in Scope and it has rows, Scope uses it in place of the whole of the workbook's Ownership sheet. It only defines views and never changes the four input sheets.
example: If the workbook's Ownership sheet says Investor 5 = 10% and the grid edited in Scope says 100%, Scope uses 100%.

confirm: When you edit the grid in Scope, should it replace the whole Ownership tab rather than just the cells you changed? Later edits to the workbook's Ownership tab would then be ignored.

title: Maturity buckets can be typed as a list
rule: When maturity buckets are typed as text, Scope splits them at commas or semicolons and ignores spaces around each one.
example: "0-5, 5-10, 10+" gives the buckets 0-5, 5-10 and 10+.
code: if (typeof S.maturityBuckets === 'string') S.maturityBuckets = SETTING_KEYS.maturitybuckets[1](S.maturityBuckets);
tests: settings: a duplicated Investors row is reported and the first kept; a formula coefficient above 1 is a multiple while an ownership above 1 is a percentage; maturity buckets typed as text work
confirm: Is a list separated by commas or semicolons the right way to type maturity buckets?

title: An empty bucket list reverts to the standard buckets
rule: If the maturity buckets are missing or empty after reading, Scope uses the standard 0-3, 3-5, 5-10, 10-20 and 20+ buckets.
example: Typing "," as the Maturity buckets setting gives the standard buckets.
code: if (!Array.isArray(S.maturityBuckets) || !S.maturityBuckets.length) S.maturityBuckets = CONFIG.maturityBuckets;
confirm: Should an empty bucket list quietly revert to the standard buckets, or be reported on Data › Issues so you notice?

title: The FX quote chosen in Scope always wins
rule: An FX quote chosen in Scope, including automatic, overrides the Scope Settings sheet and Scope's built-in setting.
example: If the sheet says FX quote "Auto" and you chose currency per EUR in Scope, Scope divides by the rate.
code: if (ov.fxQuote) S.fxQuote = ov.fxQuote; // an override (including 'auto') wins
tests: FX: the workbook rule uses one rate per currency (the reference investor's first row); a currency it does not hold falls back with a warning
confirm: Should the FX quote set in Scope override the workbook's setting? The workbook's choice is ignored for as long as the change in Scope stands.

title: Name of the Scope Settings tab
rule: Scope reads the older settings sheet from the tab named "Scope Settings". Capitals, spaces, underscores and hyphens in the tab name don't matter.
example: A tab named "scope_settings" is read as Scope Settings.

tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
confirm: Is the Scope Settings tab still needed now that the Ownership tab exists? If not, it could be dropped so ownership lives in one place.

rule: Scope finds each table on the Scope Settings sheet by its title cell. Investors table: "Investors", "Investor columns", "Group ownership" or "Ownership". Views table: "Views", "Weights", "View weights", "Investor weights" or "View formulas". FX table: "FX Exception" or "FX Exceptions". Settings table: "Settings". Capitals and punctuation don't matter.

tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere
confirm: Are these titles enough? A table under any other title would not be read.

title: Column headers of the Investors table
rule: Scope finds the Investors table's columns by their headers. Investor column: "Investor column", "Investor", "Holdings Name" or "Column". Type: "Type", "Investor type" or "Class". Display name: "Display name", "Name" or "Shown as". If several columns match, Scope uses the leftmost.

title: Which header marks the ownership column
rule: Scope takes as the Investors table's ownership column any header containing "ownership", "weight", "attribut" or "share". A header of just "%" is not recognised.
example: A column headed "Group share" or "Attribution weight" is read as ownership; a column headed "%" is not.

title: Column headers for view formulas
rule: In the formula layout of the Views table, Scope looks for a "View" column and a "Formula", "Definition" or "Composition" column.
example: A row with View "Region A" and Definition "Investor 3 + Investor 4" defines Region A.

rule: Scope finds the FX Exception columns by their headers. Investor: "Investor", "Portfolio", "Investor or portfolio code" or "Investor code". Then "Currency", "View", rate ("Rate" or "Rate or Hardcoded column") and "Note".

title: Type and Display name rows in the matrix layout
rule: In the matrix layout of the Views table, Scope reads a row named "Type", "Investor type" or "Class" as each column's investor type, and a row named "Display name", "Display names", "Name" or "Shown as" as each column's display name.
example: A "Type" row reading "Group entity" under Investor 1 and "Fund" under Fund 1 makes Investor 1 a Group entity and Fund 1 a Fund.

title: Names that mark the group row
rule: Scope treats a row or view named Group, Group weights, Group weight, Attribution, Attribution weights, Attributed, or the attribution label you set, as the group (attribution) row. Capitals and punctuation don't matter.
example: A row named "group weights" is read as the group row.

tests: Scope Settings sheet: app changes beat the sheet, the sheet beats the defaults, and names can be changed everywhere

rule: The Settings table understands only these settings: attribution label, IG threshold, base currency, FX quote, nominal in, drawn in, commitment in, look-through drawn, FX rate source, FX reference investor, spread unit, the SINGLE word (row name "Single portfolio token") and maturity buckets. title: Reading attribution label, IG threshold and base currency
rule: Scope reads "Attribution label" as text, ignoring spaces at either end. It reads "IG threshold" as a number, ignoring thousand separators, % and currency signs. It reads "Base currency" as text in capitals, ignoring spaces at either end.
example: Base currency " gbp " is read as GBP; IG threshold "610" is read as 610.

title: How the FX quote setting is worded
rule: Scope reads the FX quote setting from its words, and capitals don't matter. Anything containing "auto" means automatic. Otherwise "EUR per", "×", "multiply" or "eurperccy" means multiply by the rate, and "per EUR", "÷", "divide" or "ccyper" means divide by the rate. Scope ignores anything else and warns.

title: The internal rating column

title: The closing rating column

title: Watchlist wordings that mean "off"
rule: Scope treats a watchlist value as off when it is blank; when it is exactly No, N, None, Nil, Off, OK, Okay, Clear, Normal, Standard, Regular, Performing, Green, N/A, NA, "-", "–", 0 or False; when it starts with the word No, Not, Non, Off, "Removed from", "Taken off" or "Cleared"; or when it ends with ":", "=", "-" or "–" followed by No, None, Off, False or 0. Capitals don't matter. A "No", "Not" or "Non" at the start does not make a value off when "perform" follows: "Non-performing" and "Not performing" are on.
example: "Performing", "Not on watchlist", "No watch", "Off watch", "Removed from watchlist", "Watchlist: No" and "-" all mean not on the watchlist.
code: ^(no|not|non|off|removed from|taken off|cleared)\b(?!.?perform)
tests: watchlist: only values that say watch / intensive / yes count; Performing, Not on watchlist, blank do not; the values seen are listed
oracle: distributions, shares and labels (position-level currency and rate type, Mixed / Multi, buckets, watchlist, decimal-comma weight)
confirm: Is this the right list of "not on the watchlist" wordings? Any other value that mentions watch, red, amber and the like counts as on the watchlist.

title: Watchlist wordings that mean "on"
rule: Scope counts a value that is not an off wording as on the watchlist when it contains, as a whole word, watch (or watchlist and similar), intensive, yes, amber, red, orange, monitor (or monitoring and similar), alert, special, enhanced, under review or true, or is exactly Y, 1 or X. Capitals don't matter; and the credit words default, impaired, distressed, workout and non-/not-/under-performing (in any form). "Cleared" and "Restructured" are not on.
example: "Watch", "Intensive care", "Amber", "Under review" and "Red flag" mean on the watchlist. "Cleared", "Restructured", "Unmonitored" and "Off watch" do not. "Non-performing", "Defaulted" and "Impaired" are on.
code: |true|default\w*|impair\w*|distress\w*|workout)\b|\b(non|not|under).?perform\w*|^(y|1|x)$/i;
tests: watchlist: only values that say watch / intensive / yes count; Performing, Not on watchlist, blank do not; the values seen are listed
confirm: Is this the right list of "on the watchlist" wordings? A value such as "Red flag removed" still counts as on the watchlist, because it contains "red" and does not start with an off wording.

title: Unclear watchlist values are not counted
rule: Scope does not count a watchlist value that is neither an on nor an off wording as on the watchlist. It lists the different values it saw on Data › Issues.
example: "Level 2" is not counted as on the watchlist, and is listed on Data › Issues.
code: AUM.onWatchlist = (v) => { const t = str(v).trim(); return !!t && !WATCH_OFF.test(t) && WATCH_ON.test(t); };
tests: watchlist: only values that say watch / intensive / yes count; Performing, Not on watchlist, blank do not; the values seen are listed
confirm: Should an unrecognised watchlist value count as on the watchlist, to be cautious, instead of off? Today a value like "Level 2" leaves the asset off the watchlist.

title: Dates typed as text, and other numbers
rule: Scope reads other dates in the forms yyyy-mm-dd, dd/mm/yyyy or dd.mm.yyyy. When the first two parts could each be the day or the month, Scope reads the day first; it reads the month first only when the second part is above 12. It also reads a five-digit Excel date number typed as text, and any other form the browser understands. A number outside 20,000 to 80,000 is read as if it were text. A time after the date ("30/09/2026 00:00:00") is dropped; a five-digit date number as text, with or without a fraction ("46295.5"), is an Excel date number; a worded date ("1 Jan 2027") is that day whatever the computer's time zone; a year outside 1900–2200 is no date.

title: Capitals, accents and "&" don't matter
rule: Before comparing names, Scope ignores capitals and accents and reads "&" as "and".

title: Percentages, decimals and years are ignored
rule: Before comparing, Scope removes decimal numbers, percentages and stand-alone years from 1900 to 2099. Letters and digits written together are split apart.
example: "Kestrel 2.5% 2030" matches "Kestrel" exactly (score 100). "Lynx2" is read as "Lynx 2".

rule: Write-ups Scope could not match to an asset (no sure match, or several assets as good) go into no report, because they cannot be placed in a view, unless the setting "Write-ups linked to no asset" is set to "in every report". The reporting and write-ups pages say how many are left out so you can link them.
example: With 3 write-ups of which one is unmatched, each report carries only the linked ones its view holds; the page says 1 write-up matches no asset.
code: R.writeupInView = (l, held, unlinked) => (l.codes.length ? l.codes.some((c) => held.has(c)) : l.target !== 'none' && unlinked === 'include');
tests: asset write-ups: every sheet read (a box per sheet, no header row), linked by name or by hand, the view's write-ups on monitoring pages like the deck's

area: Write-ups › links set by hand and which report carries them
title: "Not linked" means in no report
rule: A write-up you set to "Not linked" is in no report, whatever the setting. An ambiguous one is treated like an unmatched one (WU-116).

area: Write-ups › links set by hand and which report carries them

area: Write-ups › links set by hand and which report carries them
title: Report order follows the deal order

title: Text size shrinks for long write-ups
rule: Scope sets the text column at font size 8, at font size 7.5 when the description plus events run over 2,200 characters, and at font size 7 over 3,200 characters.

title: How much text fits on a page
rule: To split write-ups into pages, Scope assumes a text line about 17.5 cm wide in which each character is half the font size wide, with at least 30 characters a line. Each line takes 1.32 times the font size in height, and the usable height is the template's content area minus 2.3 cm (14.1 cm minus 2.3 cm without a template), never less than 5.1 cm.
example: At font size 8, a line holds about 124 characters and a page about 31 lines on the standard layout.
code: const boxH = cb.h - 0.3 - 0.6, room = Math.floor((Math.max(2, boxH) * SY * 72) / (fs * 1.32));

title: Long write-ups carry on to the next page
